name: Floating canvas suit construction

lead: A floating canvas is a layer of sturdy interfacing placed between a jacket's outer cloth and its lining, attached by stitching so that it can move with the cloth. It is the construction associated with expensive and bespoke suits.

For appearance, the appeal is the way the jacket hangs: a canvas that is not glued down is described as softer and more supple than a fused one, and tailors say it holds up better than a poorly fused one. The reference material on the topic is mostly tailoring lore rather than studies.

paras: People check a jacket's construction before buying or commissioning it, often by pinching the chest area to feel whether the layers move independently or are bonded together. A floating canvas is typically found in bespoke and made-to-measure suits and in higher-priced ready-to-wear. It is usually paired with a good fit through the shoulders and chest, since construction and fit work together.

There are no health risks; the trade-offs are cost, weight and care. Floating-canvas jackets are generally more expensive, and some sellers argue the practical gap to well-made fused jackets is small. Fused interlinings that are poorly made are reported by tailors to pucker at the edges after wear or dry cleaning.

Jacket drapes and holds shape on the torso
angle.text: A floating canvas changes how the jacket hangs and holds its shape, which affects how the torso reads in a suit. Tailors describe the result as a softer drape than fused construction.

lead: A floating canvas is the interior structure of a suit jacket in which a layer of sturdy interfacing, the canvas, sits between the outer fabric and the lining and is held in place by stitching rather than adhesive [1]. It gives the wool support so that it does not stretch out of shape [1].

For someone trying to look better dressed, the point of the construction is drape and silhouette. Tailors and writers on tailoring describe a floating canvas as softer and more supple than a glued, fused canvas [1]. Fused construction is cheaper to produce; the Wikipedia article on suits notes that poorly done fusing can reduce suppleness and durability, and that tailors often say it can pucker along the edges after wear or dry cleaning, while some sellers argue the quality difference is very small [1].

Expensive jackets are said to use a floating canvas, and some London tailors state that all bespoke suits should [1]. No clinical or controlled studies of canvas construction appear to have been published; the claims are those of tailors and the clothing trade.

paras: Canvas is a layer of sturdy interfacing between a jacket's outer cloth and lining. In a floating canvas it is sewn in so that it is free to move relative to the outer fabric, whereas a fused canvas is glued to it [1].
The Wikipedia article on suits distinguishes these two forms.

Proponents say a floating canvas produces a softer, more supple jacket. The same source reports that a poorly fused jacket can lose suppleness and durability, and that tailors say fused interlinings may pucker at the edges after wear or dry cleaning [1].
Some sellers argue the quality difference between the two is very small [1].
